title: The 8 Levels of Burnout
house: a gray concrete apartment building in downtown Chicago
links: Level 1 buys coffee from the barista in Level 4 every morning.
Level 3 reviews the expense report of Level 6.
Level 5 shares an elevator with Level 2 on Tuesday nights.
Level 7 answers emails from the boss in Level 8.

levels.open_loop: What was written on the final eviction notice taped to the glass door?

gegenspieler.tat: Refuses to accept her expired coupon and laughs at her empty card.

levels.name: Marcus, 24, Night Shift Packer
levels.story: The 8 Levels of Corporate Burnout. Level 1. 14 hours on my feet for 11 dollars an hour. My ankles are completely numb. I dropped scanner number four on the concrete floor, and my supervisor just stared at me. You're simply not working fast enough. I have zero dollars left for groceries this week. My rent went up to 1,250 dollars, and my phone screen is shattered into a spiderweb. I drink instant coffee with tap water and stare at the wall for hours before sleep. Then the manager walked over with a clipboard in his hand. What was written onด the final eviction notice taped to the glass door? You'll see that in Level 2.

levels.name: Chloe, 29, Junior Data Entry
levels.story: The 8 Levels of Corporate Burnout. Level 2. 48 spreadsheets a day while my left eye twitches constantly. I stopped answering Slack messages after 5 PM sharp. My manager walked past my cubicle and slammed a heavy binder on the desk. Just do it over from scratch. I eat cold pasta standing up in the tiny shared kitchen. My student loan payment is 450 dollars a month, and my landlord is raising rent to 1,600 dollars. I have two browser tabs open for job applications hidden behind Excel. Then my Outlook notification sound chimed in an empty office. Who sent the mysterious calendar invite for midnight? You'll see that in Level 3.

levels.name: David, 34, Mid-Level Analyst
levels.story: The 8 Levels of Corporate Burnout. Level 3. 72,000 dollars a year to stare at pivot tables until my chest tightens. My doctor asked me why my resting heart rate is 110 beats per minute. You need to learn how to manage your stress better. I pay 2,100 dollars rent for a one-bedroom apartment with zero natural light. My team lead dumped three extra client decks on my desk right before the weekend. I haven't spoken to my brother in four months because I am always too drained. Then my office phone started vibrating across the wooden desk. What did the HR director whisper into the phone? You'll see that in Level 4.

levels.name: Sarah, 31, Senior Copywriter
levels.story: The 8 Levels of Corporate Burnout. Level 4. 95,000 dollars a year and I cry in the stairwell twice every single week. I wrote forty versions of the same banner ad because the client changed their mind again. We value your passion, but this needs more pop. My therapy sessions cost 180 dollars an hour just to talk about my boss. I live in a 2,500 dollar apartment where I only sleep on weekends. My friends invited me to dinner, but I canceled because I couldn't lift my arms. Then the office printer started flashing red with an error message. Why was the entire marketing department locked out of their accounts? You'll see that in Level 5.

levels.name: Tom, 38, Project Manager
levels.story: The 8 Levels of Corporate Burnout. Level 5. 125,000 dollars a year, and I spend nine hours a day in Zoom rooms talking to black boxes. My daughter asked me why my laptop is glued to my hands during dinner. You are the glue that holds this entire division together, Tom. My mortgage is 3,200 dollars, and my property taxes just went up another notch. I haven't slept through the night in three years without taking melatonin. My calendar is color-coded so tightly there is literally no white space left. Then my phone buzzed with an urgent text from the CEO. What emergency document was hidden inside the locked desk drawer? You'll see that in Level 6.

levels.name: Elena, 42, Director of Operations
levels.story: The 8 Levels of Corporate Burnout. Level 6. 165,000 dollars a year, and I am the punching bag for both the board and the floor. My husband stopped asking about my day because I just sigh and stare at the television. We need you to lay off twenty percent of your team by Friday afternoon. My private school tuition for my kids is 2,400 dollars a month. I take sleeping pills just to get four hours of restless brain activity. My phone rings during Sunday family brunch every single week without fail. Then my printer spat out a confidential twenty-page restructuring memo. Whose name was crossed out on the restructuring org chart? You'll see that in Level 7.

levels.name: Marcus V., 49, VP of Strategy
levels.story: The 8 Levels of Corporate Burnout. Level 7. 240,000 dollars a year plus stock options, and I haven't felt joy since my promotion in 2019. My Porsche sits in the underground garage while I sleep on a cot in my corner office. You're too valuable in this chair to even think about stepping down now, Marcus. My alimony payments are 5,000 dollars a month, and my mortgage on the penthouse is 7,500 dollars. I take blood pressure medication with lukewarm tap water from the executive washroom. My entire life is filtered through quarterly earnings reports and stock tickers. Then the board chairman walked in without knocking and locked the heavy oak door. What did the board chairman whisper before locking the boardroom door? You'll see that in Level 8.

gegenspieler.tat: None. He walked out and left the entire building behind.

levels.name: Arthur, 58, Former CEO
levels.story: The 8 Levels of Corporate Burnout. Level 8. Zero dollars salary because I walked out of the glass tower and left my phone in the elevator. I am sitting on a wooden park bench with a simple cup of black coffee watching the pigeons. Congratulations, Arthur, you finally remembered what living actually feels like. My bank accounts are frozen, my penthouse is sold, and I have one small suitcase. I haven't checked my corporate email in forty-eight hours, and my chest pain completely vanished. The sun is shining directly on my face for the first time in thirty years of meetings. What was actually written inside the final envelope left on the empty desk? Which topic should we explore in our next series?
